events.title: Polymarket map tracking Ukraine war was falsely manipulated to show Russian advance before market resolution, triggering 33,000% payouts
events.summary: In November 2025, a live map tracking the Russia-Ukraine war used by Polymarket was falsely manipulated to show a Russian advance shortly before a market bet on the conflict resolved. Users had placed bets on whether Russia would capture the city of Myrnohrad by various dates, generating over $1 million in trading volume. On November 15, the map was edited to show Russian troops had taken control of an intersection in Myrnohrad. After the market resolved, the Russian advance was removed from the map. The unauthorized edit triggered payouts as high as 33,000% for those who bet Russia would gain control by November 15. The Institute for the Study of War (ISW), which provided the map, condemned the unauthorized edit and stated it "strenuously objects" to use of its maps for prediction market betting.
events.why_relevant: Manipulation of data used to resolve prediction markets on military operations demonstrates how war-related betting creates incentives for fraud and undermines market integrity while affecting real-world conflict reporting.
events.federal_nexus: Polymarket operates in the U.S. and is subject to CFTC oversight; the manipulation affected U.S. traders and the integrity of a federally-regulated market category.
events.basis: Shortly before one of the bets was set to resolve on November 15, the map that Polymarket relied on for the market was edited to show that Russian troops had taken control of an intersection in Myrnohrad. But after the market resolved, the Russian advance was removed from the map. According to Responsible Statecraft, the edit 'triggered payouts as high as 33,000%' for those who bet that Russia would gain control over the city by November 15.

events.title: EPA amends EPCRA hazardous chemical inventory reporting regulations to conform to 2024 OSHA Hazard Communication Standard
events.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency issued a direct final rule amending 40 CFR Part 370 to align Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act (EPCRA) hazardous chemical inventory reporting requirements with the Occupational Safety and Health Administration's 2024 Hazard Communication Standard (HCS) updates. The rule expands EPCRA hazard categories from 24 to 112 categories by directly incorporating OSHA's detailed hazard classifications, removes outdated references to Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS) in favor of Safety Data Sheets (SDS), relocates definitions from § 370.66 to § 370.3, and makes plain-language clarifications. The effective date is January 16, 2026, with compliance required for 2026 annual reporting (due March 1, 2027). The rule is expected to reduce administrative burden on facilities and improve first responder and community safety by providing more precise hazard information.
events.why_relevant: This regulatory amendment directly affects how thousands of industrial facilities report chemical hazards to emergency responders and communities, altering the information environment for public safety and emergency planning while reducing compliance burden through alignment with federal occupational safety standards.
events.basis: The Environmental Protection Agency is taking direct final action to conform the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act hazardous chemical inventory reporting regulations to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration's Hazard Communication Standard amendments of 2012 and 2024.

The approval follows a 60-day public comment period and a reopened 15-day comment period. North Dakota must reissue previously issued permits under the approved program to ensure compliance with federal standards.

events.title: EPA establishes pesticide tolerance for fluazinam residues on Asian pears
events.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency issued a final rule establishing a maximum permissible residue level of 0.2 parts per million for the fungicide fluazinam on Asian pears, in response to a petition by ISK Biosciences Corporation filed in December 2023. EPA determined that aggregate exposure to fluazinam residues—including dietary, drinking water, and residential exposures—poses no reasonable risk of harm to the general population, infants, or children. The tolerance is effective immediately; objections and hearing requests must be filed by January 16, 2026.

events.title: EPA establishes time-limited pesticide tolerance for chlorantraniliprole on rice under FIFRA emergency exemption

This action responds to Louisiana's emergency exemption request to control stem borer pest damage in rice production systems rotated with crawfish. The tolerance expires December 31, 2028. EPA determined the tolerance meets the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act safety standard based on risk assessment showing chronic dietary exposure will utilize only 9.3% of the chronic population-adjusted dose for the most-exposed population subgroup (children 1–2 years old).

events.title: Complaint filed — Healthy Gulf v. Burgum (D.D.C. 1:25-cv-04016)
events.summary: Environmental organizations Healthy Gulf, Friends of the Earth, Center for Biological Diversity, Natural Resources Defense Council, and Sierra Club filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia challenging the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management's November 10, 2025 Final Notice of Sale for the first of 30 Gulf of Mexico oil and gas lease sales mandated by the 2025 Reconciliation Act. events.title: Report documents systemic exploitation of formerly incarcerated workers by Florida temp agencies
events.summary: Beyond the Bars, a non-profit advocacy organization, published a report documenting how hundreds of thousands of Florida workers with criminal records are trapped in temporary staffing arrangements with lower wages, no benefits, and limited pathways to permanent employment. The report found over 70% of individuals released from prison in south Florida use temp agencies within three years, with 57% unable to secure full-time minimum-wage work within a year. Temp workers in construction earn $6.47 less per hour and warehouse workers $3.38 less per hour than permanent hires, resulting in annual income losses of $13,458 and $7,030 respectively.
